15:T26ac,<p>I wrote <a href="/v2/rust-ate-javascript-build-toolchain">a whole post</a> about how the JavaScript build toolchain got rewritten in Rust. SWC replaced Babel, Turbopack replaced Webpack, and I mapped the whole thing. But there was one line in it I just repeated without earning: <em>Rust is faster</em>.</p>
<p>Faster how? Faster by how much? I didn't know. I had passed the sentence along the way everyone does, like a coin worn smooth from being handed over so many times.</p>
<p>So I sat down and built a benchmark. I wrote down what I expected first, then ran it. Of five predictions, two held on the spot, one needed a different way of measuring, one I misread at first, and one got the mechanism wrong.</p>
<h2>It isn't one number</h2>
<p>Across seven scenarios, Rust against Node ranged from a dead tie to 37 times faster.</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-spectrum" width="100%" height="450" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:700px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Rust vs Node speed across seven scenarios"></iframe>
<p>Summing ten million floats: Node 9.556ms, Rust 9.553ms, virtually identical. A running sum is a chain, each addition waiting on the one before it, so both sides sat at the latency of a single floating-point add.</p>
<p>For churning through short-lived objects, Node's median was actually faster, because V8's generational garbage collector is designed for exactly that. New objects go into a region that gets cleared in bulk, so allocating an object is little more than moving a pointer forward by the object's size. That result contradicts my title, and I trust it most, because I didn't want it to be true.</p>
<h2>Small arrays: Node wins. Large arrays: Rust wins.</h2>
<p>The exact same loop, with only the array length changed.</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-dataflip" width="100%" height="430" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:620px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Same branch, winner flips with array size"></iframe>
<p>The loop does one small thing per number: if it clears a threshold, add it to a running total; otherwise skip it.</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="python" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="python" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">for</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> each number </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">in</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> the array:</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">    y </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> number </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">*</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> 2</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">    if</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> y </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">></span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> 1</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">:  total </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> total </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">+</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> y    </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D"># add it</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">    else</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">:      total </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> total        </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D"># skip, unchanged</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>The data is random, so that <code>if</code> is true about half the time. And to keep the sizes comparable, I held the total work constant: about 200 million element reads at every length, so a small array just gets walked many more times than a big one. The chart shows cost per element, not total time.</p>
<p>So why does the same element cost more when the array gets longer? Node and Rust compile that <code>if</code> into different machine code.</p>
<p><strong>Node keeps it as a real branch</strong>: at this point there are two paths, add or skip. The CPU doesn't wait for the comparison result; it <em>guesses</em> one path and keeps executing (branch prediction). A correct guess costs nothing extra. A wrong guess throws away the work it already ran and redoes it. On the chart, Node's cost per element rises from 0.9ns to over 5ns, and the extra time goes to redoing work after wrong guesses. The guess is based on how this branch behaved recently.</p>
<p><strong>Rust builds it with no branch at all.</strong> Its compiler, through LLVM, computes both the added total and the unchanged one, then picks the right one with a single "conditional select" instruction. On ARM64 that instruction is <code>fcsel</code> (the machine I measured on is an Apple M1 Pro). The cost is an extra addition and one more register every time; with no branch, the CPU has nothing to guess:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="asm" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="asm" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">fadd</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">   d2, total, y      </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; compute total + y no matter what</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">fcmp   y, threshold      </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; compare</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">fcsel  total, d2, total  </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; take total+y if it cleared the bar, else keep total</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>How often Node's guesses hit depends on the array length:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Small array</strong>: the short sequence of add/skip gets walked over and over, so the whole sequence fits within what the branch predictor can record, and it guesses right nearly every time. Cheap. Random doesn't stop this; a short fixed sequence, even one that looks random, gets recorded in full after a few passes.</li>
<li><strong>Large array</strong>: the sequence is longer than the branch predictor can record, so it guesses wrong about half the time, and every miss means redoing the work. Expensive.</li>
</ul>
<p>Rust never guesses, so its cost per element is the same at every size (the flat line on the chart). "Rust is faster on unpredictable branches" only holds when the array is longer than the branch predictor can record.</p>
<h2>So where do the 20-70x claims come from?</h2>
<p>SWC says it's <a href="https://swc.rs/">20x faster than Babel on one thread, 70x on four cores</a>. If a single-threaded language gap is only around three times, where does the rest come from?</p>
<p>To separate the language from native compilation plus new architecture, I added esbuild for comparison. It's written in Go, not Rust, but it too is compiled to a native binary and designed from scratch.</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-esbuild" width="100%" height="310" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:620px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Babel vs SWC vs esbuild compile time"></iframe>
<p>esbuild compiles in 26.3ms and SWC in 19.6ms, the same order of magnitude, both far ahead of Babel. So the big multiple is reachable in Go too; it doesn't need Rust. In the same-algorithm test in the first chart, an identical tree walk, JS against native differs by only 2.7x. That 2.7x comes from compiling to native or not; it is the part the language itself accounts for, and it is small. Babel against SWC measured 8x to 51x, depending on whether the target is ES2019 or ES5; what is left after the 2.7x is architecture, Babel's visitor pattern, plugin pipeline, and constant node rebuilding, and that has nothing to do with which language.</p>
<p>And the "four cores" half of the 70x isn't Rust either. On the same work, eight threads made Node 5.8x faster and Rust 6.3x, so both sides can use multiple cores. Node runs JavaScript, the same language as Babel, and its built-in worker threads spread the work across every core. Babel uses one core because it never implemented this.</p>
<h2>Breaking down the 20 to 70x</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>About 3x</strong>: leaving JavaScript for a native binary. A build tool runs once and exits, so a JIT never warms up in time.</li>
<li><strong>The biggest piece, architecture</strong>: Babel walks the tree once per plugin and keeps rebuilding nodes; SWC was designed from scratch. It grows with the work: switch the target from ES2019 to ES5 and Babel's own time grows 27x, while SWC's grows only 4.6x.</li>
<li><strong>About 3.5x, cores</strong> (SWC's own 20x to 70x): Babel never used them, even though Node has worker threads available.</li>
</ul>
<p>Native compilation, a redesigned architecture, and parallelism, three factors and not one of them is Rust. Rust is a fine language to build these in. It just isn't the reason they got fast.</p>
<p>The toolchain story that started all this is <a href="/v2/rust-ate-javascript-build-toolchain">here</a>.</p>16:T1b1b,
I wrote [a whole post](/v2/rust-ate-javascript-build-toolchain) about how the JavaScript build toolchain got rewritten in Rust. SWC replaced Babel, Turbopack replaced Webpack, and I mapped the whole thing. But there was one line in it I just repeated without earning: *Rust is faster*.

Faster how? Faster by how much? I didn't know. I had passed the sentence along the way everyone does, like a coin worn smooth from being handed over so many times.

So I sat down and built a benchmark. I wrote down what I expected first, then ran it. Of five predictions, two held on the spot, one needed a different way of measuring, one I misread at first, and one got the mechanism wrong.

## It isn't one number

Across seven scenarios, Rust against Node ranged from a dead tie to 37 times faster.

<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-spectrum" width="100%" height="450" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:700px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Rust vs Node speed across seven scenarios"></iframe>

Summing ten million floats: Node 9.556ms, Rust 9.553ms, virtually identical. A running sum is a chain, each addition waiting on the one before it, so both sides sat at the latency of a single floating-point add.

For churning through short-lived objects, Node's median was actually faster, because V8's generational garbage collector is designed for exactly that. New objects go into a region that gets cleared in bulk, so allocating an object is little more than moving a pointer forward by the object's size. That result contradicts my title, and I trust it most, because I didn't want it to be true.

## Small arrays: Node wins. Large arrays: Rust wins.

The exact same loop, with only the array length changed.

<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-dataflip" width="100%" height="430" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:620px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Same branch, winner flips with array size"></iframe>

The loop does one small thing per number: if it clears a threshold, add it to a running total; otherwise skip it.

```python
for each number in the array:
    y = number * 2
    if y > 1:  total = total + y    # add it
    else:      total = total        # skip, unchanged
```

The data is random, so that `if` is true about half the time. And to keep the sizes comparable, I held the total work constant: about 200 million element reads at every length, so a small array just gets walked many more times than a big one. The chart shows cost per element, not total time.

So why does the same element cost more when the array gets longer? Node and Rust compile that `if` into different machine code.

**Node keeps it as a real branch**: at this point there are two paths, add or skip. The CPU doesn't wait for the comparison result; it *guesses* one path and keeps executing (branch prediction). A correct guess costs nothing extra. A wrong guess throws away the work it already ran and redoes it. On the chart, Node's cost per element rises from 0.9ns to over 5ns, and the extra time goes to redoing work after wrong guesses. The guess is based on how this branch behaved recently.

**Rust builds it with no branch at all.** Its compiler, through LLVM, computes both the added total and the unchanged one, then picks the right one with a single "conditional select" instruction. On ARM64 that instruction is `fcsel` (the machine I measured on is an Apple M1 Pro). The cost is an extra addition and one more register every time; with no branch, the CPU has nothing to guess:

```asm
fadd   d2, total, y      ; compute total + y no matter what
fcmp   y, threshold      ; compare
fcsel  total, d2, total  ; take total+y if it cleared the bar, else keep total
```

How often Node's guesses hit depends on the array length:

- **Small array**: the short sequence of add/skip gets walked over and over, so the whole sequence fits within what the branch predictor can record, and it guesses right nearly every time. Cheap. Random doesn't stop this; a short fixed sequence, even one that looks random, gets recorded in full after a few passes.
- **Large array**: the sequence is longer than the branch predictor can record, so it guesses wrong about half the time, and every miss means redoing the work. Expensive.

Rust never guesses, so its cost per element is the same at every size (the flat line on the chart). "Rust is faster on unpredictable branches" only holds when the array is longer than the branch predictor can record.

## So where do the 20-70x claims come from?

SWC says it's [20x faster than Babel on one thread, 70x on four cores](https://swc.rs/). If a single-threaded language gap is only around three times, where does the rest come from?

To separate the language from native compilation plus new architecture, I added esbuild for comparison. It's written in Go, not Rust, but it too is compiled to a native binary and designed from scratch.

<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-esbuild" width="100%" height="310" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:620px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Babel vs SWC vs esbuild compile time"></iframe>

esbuild compiles in 26.3ms and SWC in 19.6ms, the same order of magnitude, both far ahead of Babel. So the big multiple is reachable in Go too; it doesn't need Rust. In the same-algorithm test in the first chart, an identical tree walk, JS against native differs by only 2.7x. That 2.7x comes from compiling to native or not; it is the part the language itself accounts for, and it is small. Babel against SWC measured 8x to 51x, depending on whether the target is ES2019 or ES5; what is left after the 2.7x is architecture, Babel's visitor pattern, plugin pipeline, and constant node rebuilding, and that has nothing to do with which language.

And the "four cores" half of the 70x isn't Rust either. On the same work, eight threads made Node 5.8x faster and Rust 6.3x, so both sides can use multiple cores. Node runs JavaScript, the same language as Babel, and its built-in worker threads spread the work across every core. Babel uses one core because it never implemented this.

## Breaking down the 20 to 70x

- **About 3x**: leaving JavaScript for a native binary. A build tool runs once and exits, so a JIT never warms up in time.
- **The biggest piece, architecture**: Babel walks the tree once per plugin and keeps rebuilding nodes; SWC was designed from scratch. It grows with the work: switch the target from ES2019 to ES5 and Babel's own time grows 27x, while SWC's grows only 4.6x.
- **About 3.5x, cores** (SWC's own 20x to 70x): Babel never used them, even though Node has worker threads available.

Native compilation, a redesigned architecture, and parallelism, three factors and not one of them is Rust. Rust is a fine language to build these in. It just isn't the reason they got fast.

The toolchain story that started all this is [here](/v2/rust-ate-javascript-build-toolchain).
17:T2698,:T2414,<p>我寫過<a href="/v2/rust-ate-javascript-build-toolchain">一整篇</a>，講 JavaScript 的 build 工具怎麼一層一層被 Rust 重寫。SWC 換掉 Babel，Turbopack 換掉 Webpack，整個過程我都梳理過了。但裡面有一句我只是照著講，沒有自己弄懂：<em>Rust 比較快</em>。</p>
<p>快在哪？快多少？我不知道，也從沒認真想過它到底是什麼意思。</p>
<p>所以我坐下來寫了一套 benchmark。我先把預期寫下來，再跑。五個預測裡，兩個當場成立，一個要換量測方法，一個我一開始讀錯，一個機制猜錯。</p>
<h2>「Rust 比較快」不是一個數字</h2>
<p>七種情況量下來，Rust 對 Node 從一樣快到快 37 倍都有。</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-spectrum" width="100%" height="450" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:700px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Rust 對 Node 的速度，七種情況"></iframe>
<p>一千萬個浮點數相加，Node 9.556ms、Rust 9.553ms，幾乎一樣。這種加總每一步都要用到上一步的結果（s = s + 這一筆），只能一個接一個做、沒辦法同時算，兩邊都卡在一次浮點加法的延遲上。</p>
<p>大量用完就丟的小物件，Node 的中位數反而比較快，因為 V8 的垃圾回收（generational GC）專門為這種情況設計。新物件都先放進一塊很快就整批清掉的區，所以配置一個物件，幾乎只是把指標往後移一個物件的大小。這個結果跟標題相反，我反而最相信它，因為我本來不希望它成立。</p>
<h2>小陣列 Node 快，大陣列 Rust 快</h2>
<p>同一段 code，只改陣列長度。</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-dataflip" width="100%" height="430" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:620px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="同一個判斷，小陣列 Node 快、大陣列 Rust 快"></iframe>
<p>這迴圈對每個數字只做一個判斷：過了門檻就加進總和，沒過就跳過。</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="python" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="python" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">掃過陣列裡每個數字:</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">    y </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> 數字 </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">*</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> 2</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">    如果 y </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">></span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> 1</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">:  total </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> total </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">+</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> y    </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D"># 加進去</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">    否則:        total </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> total        </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D"># 跳過,不變</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>資料是亂數，所以那個 <code>if</code> 大約一半成立、一半不成立。而且為了讓不同長度能公平比，我把<strong>總工作量固定住</strong>：不管陣列多大，總共都讀取約兩億個元素，所以小陣列只是被重複走比較多遍而已。圖上畫的是<strong>每個元素的成本</strong>，不是總時間。</p>
<p>為什麼陣列變長，同一個元素就花更多時間呢？差別在 Node 跟 Rust 把那個 <code>if</code> 編譯成的機器碼不一樣。</p>
<p><strong>Node 把它留成一個真的分支</strong>，執行到這裡有兩條路，加進去或跳過。CPU 不等比較結果出來，<strong>先猜</strong>一條往下執行（branch prediction）。猜對沒有額外成本；猜錯，剛剛先做的白做、要倒回重來。圖上 Node 每個元素從 0.9ns 升到 5ns 多，多出來的時間花在猜錯後重來。它猜的依據，是這個分支最近都往哪走。</p>
<p><strong>Rust 這邊乾脆讓分支消失。</strong> 它的編譯器透過 LLVM，把「加了的」跟「沒加的」都先算出來，再用一個「二選一」的指令挑對的那個。這個指令在 ARM64 上叫 <code>fcsel</code>（我測的機器是 Apple M1 Pro）。代價是每次都多算一次加法、多占一個 register；沒有分支，CPU 就沒有東西要猜：</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="asm" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="asm" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">fadd</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">   d2, total, y      </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; 條件先不管,total + y 先算好</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">fcmp   y, 門檻           </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; 比一下</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">fcsel  total, d2, total  </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">; 過門檻就挑 total+y,否則留原本的 total</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>Node 那邊猜中的比例，跟陣列長度有關：</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>小陣列</strong>：那串「加/跳」很短，被重複走很多遍 → 整串長度在分支預測器能記錄的範圍內 → 幾乎每次猜對 → 便宜。亂數不影響這件事：一串固定的短序列，就算看起來隨機，重複走幾遍，預測器就記錄到整串。</li>
<li><strong>大陣列</strong>：那串太長，超過分支預測器能記錄的長度 → 大約一半猜錯 → 每錯一次就要倒回重來 → 貴。</li>
</ul>
<p>Rust 從不猜，所以不管陣列多大，每個元素的成本都一樣（圖上就是那條水平的線）。「Rust 在難猜的分支上比較快」這句話，只在陣列長到超過分支預測器能記錄的長度時成立。</p>
<h2>那 20 到 70 倍到底哪來的</h2>
<p>SWC 說它<a href="https://swc.rs/">單執行緒比 Babel 快 20 倍、四核心快 70 倍</a>。如果單執行緒的語言差只有三倍上下，剩下的是哪來的？</p>
<p>為了把「語言」跟「原生加新架構」分開，再拿 esbuild 對照。它是 Go 寫的，不是 Rust，但一樣編譯成原生執行檔、一樣是從頭設計的新工具。</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/rust-bench-esbuild" width="100%" height="310" loading="lazy" style="border:0;overflow:hidden;max-width:620px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto;" title="Babel 對 SWC 對 esbuild 的編譯時間"></iframe>
<p>esbuild 編譯要 26.3ms，SWC 要 19.6ms，同一個量級，都遠快過 Babel。所以那個大倍數用 Go 也能達成，不一定要 Rust。前面圖裡同演算法那組，一模一樣的樹走訪，JS 對原生只差 2.7 倍。這 2.7 倍來自有沒有編譯成原生，是語言本身佔的部分，只是一小部分。Babel 對 SWC 實測是 8 到 51 倍，看編譯目標是 ES2019 還是 ES5；扣掉那 2.7 倍，多出來的才是架構（Babel 的 visitor pattern、plugin pipeline、大量重建節點），跟哪個語言無關。</p>
<p>那個 70 倍裡的「四核心」也不是 Rust 的。同一份工作，八執行緒讓 Node 快 5.8 倍、Rust 快 6.3 倍，兩邊都能利用多核心。Node 跑的就是 JavaScript，跟 Babel 同一個語言，用內建的 worker threads 就能把工作分到每個核心。Babel 只用一個核心，是因為它沒實作這一塊。</p>
<h2>20 到 70 倍拆開來看</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>大概 3 倍</strong>：離開 JavaScript、換成原生執行檔。build 工具跑一次就結束，JIT 來不及暖機。</li>
<li><strong>最大因素，架構</strong>：Babel 每個 plugin 走訪一遍樹、一路重建節點，SWC 從頭設計。這一塊隨工作量放大：目標從 ES2019 換成 ES5，Babel 比自己原本慢了 27 倍，SWC 只慢 4.6 倍。</li>
<li><strong>約 3.5 倍，多核心</strong>（SWC 自己的 20 倍到 70 倍）：Babel 從來沒用，雖然 Node 有 worker threads 可以用。</li>
</ul>
<p>原生執行檔、架構重寫、多核心，三個因子，沒有一個是 Rust 這個語言。Rust 是拿來做這些工具的好語言，只是它不是它們變快的原因。</p>
